did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with a command to keep the father’s words and commandments, presenting listening and obedience as the foundation of spiritual and moral protection.
The commandments and teaching are described as something to guard like the pupil of the eye—something precious and delicate that requires special protection.
The expressions “Tie them to your fingers” and “Write them on the tablet of your heart” emphasize that it is not enough to hear outwardly; wisdom must become a lasting part of who you are.
Wisdom and understanding are presented through images of family closeness: “my sister” and “my intimate friend.” In this way, the chapter encourages a close and personal relationship with wisdom.
At this point, the perspective changes: the father says that he watched from his house what was happening outside and describes the danger by observing a young man going toward the woman’s house.
The woman is described as “dressed as a prostitute and crafty of heart.” This portrays her as someone who acts through seduction and deception, rather than as someone quietly remaining at home.

The woman uses religious language to seduce him: she mentions peace offerings and vows that she has paid. In this way, the temptation combines an appearance of respectability with a forbidden invitation.
The chapter emphasizes the power of persuasive speech: through “much seductive talk” and “the smoothness of her lips,” she leads the young man away from the right path.

The young man is compared to an ox led to the slaughter and a bird hurrying into a snare. Both comparisons emphasize that he is moving toward danger without understanding the consequences of his actions.

The chapter ends with a stark conclusion: the woman’s house is described as a road descending to Sheol and the chambers of death. The warning is therefore not merely against a momentary stumble, but against a destructive path.
